questions.stem: Price elasticity of demand is calculated as

options.text: change in quantity demanded divided by change in price
percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price
percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded
total revenue divided by quantity demanded

questions.explanation: Elasticity must compare proportionate changes, because absolute changes depend on the units used. Using percentages makes the answer a pure number that can be compared across goods measured in kilogrammes, litres or crates.

distractorRationale.a: Using absolute changes gives an answer that changes if you switch from kilogrammes to tonnes
distractorRationale.c: This inverts the formula and would give 2 where the correct answer is 0.5
distractorRationale.d: Total revenue divided by quantity is average revenue, in other words the price

questions.stem: When the price of a commodity falls from ₦250 to ₦200, quantity demanded rises from 400 units to 500 units. Calculate the price elasticity of demand, giving your answer as a positive number.
questions.explanation: The percentage change in price is −50 ÷ 250 × 100 = −20 per cent, and the percentage change in quantity is 100 ÷ 400 × 100 = 25 per cent. PED is therefore 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25, so demand is elastic.

questions.stem: The price of a bucket of garri rises from ₦500 to ₦600 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 180 buckets. Demand for garri is therefore
questions.explanation: Price rose by 20 per cent while quantity demanded fell by only 10 per cent, so PED = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5. Since the value is between 0 and 1, quantity responded proportionately less than price and demand is inelastic.

distractorRationale.a: Perfectly inelastic demand would mean quantity stayed at 200 buckets
distractorRationale.c: Unitary elasticity would require a 20 per cent fall in quantity, that is down to 160 buckets
distractorRationale.d: PED = 2 comes from inverting the formula and dividing 20 by 10

questions.stem: If the demand for a product is price inelastic, a firm that raises its price will find that total revenue
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand the percentage loss of sales is smaller than the percentage gain in price, so price times quantity rises. This is why sellers of necessities gain from price increases.

distractorRationale.b: Revenue falls after a price rise only when demand is elastic
distractorRationale.c: Revenue is roughly unchanged only at unitary elasticity
distractorRationale.d: Revenue would fall to zero only with perfectly elastic demand, which is a theoretical extreme

questions.stem: A household's monthly income rises from ₦50,000 to ₦60,000 and its purchase of beef rises from 4 kg to 5 kg. Calculate the income elasticity of demand for beef.
questions.explanation: Income rose by 10,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 20 per cent while quantity rose by 1 ÷ 4 × 100 = 25 per cent, so YED = 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25. Being positive and greater than one, beef is a normal good behaving as a luxury for this household.

questions.stem: The price of butter rises by 10 per cent and the quantity of margarine demanded rises by 20 per cent. The cross elasticity of demand is

options.text: +2, showing that the goods are substitutes
−2, showing that the goods are complements
+0.5, showing that the goods are substitutes
zero, showing that the goods are unrelated

questions.explanation: Cross elasticity is 20 ÷ 10 = +2. The positive sign is the key: buyers moved towards margarine as butter became dearer, which is the defining behaviour of substitutes.

distractorRationale.b: A negative value would mean demand for margarine fell, which happens with complements
distractorRationale.c: +0.5 comes from inverting the formula and dividing 10 by 20
distractorRationale.d: Zero would mean the demand for margarine did not respond at all

questions.stem: A good for which income elasticity of demand is negative is described as
questions.explanation: Negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises. Households abandon such goods for better substitutes once they can afford them, which is exactly what defines an inferior good.

distractorRationale.a: Normal goods have positive income elasticity
distractorRationale.b: Luxuries have income elasticity greater than one, and are therefore strongly positive
distractorRationale.d: A free good is one that is abundant and unpriced, which is a separate idea altogether

questions.stem: When the price of a crate of eggs rises from ₦300 to ₦360, quantity supplied rises from 50 crates to 65 crates. Calculate the price elasticity of supply.
questions.explanation: Price rose by 60 ÷ 300 × 100 = 20 per cent and quantity supplied rose by 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30 per cent, so PES = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5. A value above one means supply is elastic, so producers responded strongly to the price incentive.

questions.stem: Which commodity is likely to have the most inelastic demand?

options.text: One particular brand of instant noodles
Air tickets for a holiday trip

questions.explanation: Salt has almost no substitutes, takes a tiny share of household income, is a necessity in cooking and cannot easily be postponed. All four determinants point the same way, so quantity barely responds to price.

distractorRationale.a: A single brand faces many close substitutes on the same shelf, so its demand is very elastic
distractorRationale.c: A holiday flight is a postponable luxury, so demand is elastic
distractorRationale.d: A television takes a large share of income and its purchase can be delayed, making demand elastic

questions.stem: When an indirect tax is imposed on a good whose demand is inelastic, most of the tax burden is borne by the consumer.
questions.explanation: True. Inelastic demand means buyers have few alternatives, so the seller can pass most of the tax into the price without losing many sales. This is why petroleum products, tobacco and alcohol are favourite targets for indirect taxation.

distractorRationale.b: The producer bears the larger share only where demand is elastic and raising the price would drive buyers away
